# Worker Helm chart examples

Use these worker configuration variations — ingress, intermediate, and egress topologies, DNS-based addressing, and registration methods — to adapt a worker to your network position. They assume a Boundary controller or HCP Boundary cluster already exists.

| Topology | Accepts connections from | Typical Service type | Needs `public_addr` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ingress | Downstream workers and clients | `LoadBalancer` | Yes |
| Intermediate | Upstream and downstream workers | `LoadBalancer` | Yes |
| Egress | Upstream or intermediate workers; connects to targets | `ClusterIP` | No |

The operations listener uses TLS by default. Before you install an example, create the `boundary-worker-tls` Secret with `tls.crt` and `tls.key` in the release namespace:

```shell-session
$ kubectl create namespace boundary
$ kubectl create secret tls boundary-worker-tls \
  --namespace boundary \
  --cert=worker-ops.crt \
  --key=worker-ops.key
```

## Worker with ingress capabilities

An ingress worker accepts connections from downstream workers and clients. It commonly uses the controller cluster as its upstream and exposes the proxy listener publicly through a `LoadBalancer` Service.

Example HCL for a worker with ingress capabilities:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = "boundary-worker.example.com:9202"
  initial_upstreams = ["<boundary-controller-cluster:9201>"]

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "ingress"]
  }
}

kms "aead" {
  purpose = "worker-auth"
  aead_type = "aes-gcm"
  key = "ATTK2pMjMTEJGlAkUJAePnFMlNLQaXBnhSqJHVlJeKQ="
  key_id = "global_worker-auth"
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Add the HCL above to `worker.config` in `ingress-values.yaml`, then add the following values for a public LoadBalancer:

```yaml
worker:
  service:
    proxy:
      type: LoadBalancer
      port: 9202
      targetPort: 9202
    ops:
      type: ClusterIP
      port: 9203
      targetPort: 9203
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: false
    recording:
      enabled: false
```

Install the worker Helm chart:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values ingress-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

If you do not know the `public_addr` until the load balancer is created, wait for the external address:

```shell-session
$ kubectl get svc boundary-worker-proxy --namespace boundary --watch
```

Example output:

<CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

```
NAME                     TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)          AGE
boundary-worker-proxy    LoadBalancer   10.0.0.30      <pending>       9202:31600/TCP   10s
boundary-worker-proxy    LoadBalancer   10.0.0.30      203.0.113.20    9202:31600/TCP   45s
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

Update `public_addr` in `worker.config` inside `ingress-values.yaml`, and then upgrade using the same values file:

```shell-session
$ helm upgrade boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --values ingress-values.yaml \
  --rollback-on-failure \
  --wait
```

## Worker with intermediate capabilities

A worker with intermediate capabilities relays traffic between upstream and downstream workers. It requires both `initial_upstreams` and `public_addr`.

Example HCL for a worker with intermediate capabilities:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = "<intermediate-worker-address>:9202"
  initial_upstreams = ["<ingress-or-intermediate-worker-address>:9202"]

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "intermediate"]
  }
}

kms "aead" {
  purpose = "worker-auth"
  aead_type = "aes-gcm"
  key = "ATTK2pMjMTEJGlAkUJAePnFMlNLQaXBnhSqJHVlJeKQ="
  key_id = "global_worker-auth"
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Add the HCL above to `worker.config` in `intermediate-values.yaml`, then add the following values for a LoadBalancer:

```yaml
worker:
  service:
    proxy:
      type: LoadBalancer
      port: 9202
      targetPort: 9202
    ops:
      type: ClusterIP
      port: 9203
      targetPort: 9203
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: false
    recording:
      enabled: false
```

Install the worker Helm chart:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values intermediate-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

If you do not know the `public_addr` until the load balancer is created, wait for the external address (refer to the example output shown in [Worker with ingress capabilities](#worker-with-ingress-capabilities)):

```shell-session
$ kubectl get svc boundary-worker-proxy --namespace boundary --watch
```

Update `public_addr` in `worker.config` inside `intermediate-values.yaml`, then upgrade using the same values file:

```shell-session
$ helm upgrade boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --values intermediate-values.yaml \
  --rollback-on-failure \
  --wait
```

## Worker with egress capabilities

A worker with egress capabilities connects to target systems and is usually the final hop before a target. It often does not need a `public_addr`.

Example HCL for a worker with egress capabilities:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["<ingress-or-intermediate-worker-address>:9202"]

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "egress"]
  }
}

kms "aead" {
  purpose = "worker-auth"
  aead_type = "aes-gcm"
  key = "ATTK2pMjMTEJGlAkUJAePnFMlNLQaXBnhSqJHVlJeKQ="
  key_id = "global_worker-auth"
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Add the HCL above to `worker.config` in `egress-values.yaml`, then add the following values:

```yaml
worker:
  service:
    proxy:
      type: ClusterIP
      port: 9202
      targetPort: 9202
    ops:
      type: ClusterIP
      port: 9203
      targetPort: 9203
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: false
    recording:
      enabled: false
```

Install the worker with a values file that includes the worker configuration:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values egress-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

## Worker with a pre-configured DNS address

If you already control the DNS name for the worker, set `public_addr` during installation:

```hcl
worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = "boundary-worker.example.com:9202"
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "ingress"]
  }
}

kms "aead" {
  purpose = "worker-auth"
  aead_type = "aes-gcm"
  key = "<base64-encoded-32-byte-key>"
  key_id = "<worker-auth-key-id>"
}
```

After the Service receives an external address, point the DNS record to that address. This avoids changing the worker HCL after installation, but you remain responsible for ensuring that DNS resolves to the reachable worker endpoint.

## Worker-led registration

For worker-led registration, install the worker without a controller-generated activation token. The worker generates identity material at startup and writes registration information to the pod logs. For more information, see [Worker-led registration](/boundary/docs/workers/registration/worker-led).

Example HCL for worker-led registration:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]
  auth_storage_path = "/var/lib/boundary"

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "worker-led"]
  }
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Example values for worker-led registration with auth storage persistence:

```yaml
worker:
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: true
      size: 1Gi
```

The typical workflow is as follows:

1. Install the worker chart with worker-led registration settings in `worker.config`.
2. Read the worker pod logs.
3. Register or authorize the emitted worker registration information with Boundary.
4. Confirm the worker becomes active.

View logs:

```shell-session
$ kubectl logs --namespace boundary deployment/boundary-worker-deployment
```

Keep auth storage enabled for worker-led registration so the generated worker identity persists across restarts.

## Controller-led registration

The typical workflow for controller-led registration is as follows. For more details about controller-led registration, refer to [Controller-led registration](/boundary/docs/workers/registration/controller-led):

1. Create the worker resource in Boundary or HCP Boundary.
2. Obtain the controller-generated activation token.
3. Supply the token using one of the methods below.
4. Install the worker Helm chart.
5. Confirm the worker registers and persists its credentials to auth storage.

The worker uses the activation token during initial bootstrap. After successful registration, the worker uses persisted credentials from auth storage.

The chart supports three ways to supply the activation token.

<Note>

The plaintext and `extraEnv` methods store the token in the Helm release Secret, and plaintext also stores it in the ConfigMap. Use the Kubernetes Secret method to avoid storing the token in either location. Plaintext and `extraEnv` are allowed only when `secretRefs.secretName` is unset.

</Note>

### Plaintext token

Embed the token directly in `worker.config`. Suitable for development only — the token is visible to anyone who can read the ConfigMap or Helm release Secret. Do not set `secretRefs.secretName` when using this method.

Example HCL:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]
  auth_storage_path = "/var/lib/boundary"
  controller_generated_activation_token = "<activation-token>"

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "controller-led"]
  }
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Example values:

```yaml
worker:
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: true
      size: 1Gi
```

Install the worker Helm chart:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

### Token via extraEnv

Set `controller_generated_activation_token` to the `env://` reference in `worker.config` and supply the token as a key-value pair in `extraEnv`. This stores the token in the Helm release Secret, so prefer a Kubernetes Secret and do not set `secretRefs.secretName` when using this method:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]
  auth_storage_path = "/var/lib/boundary"
  controller_generated_activation_token = "env://BOUNDARY_WORKER_CONTROLLER_GENERATED_ACTIVATION_TOKEN"

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "controller-led"]
  }
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

Example values:

```yaml
extraEnv:
  - name: BOUNDARY_WORKER_CONTROLLER_GENERATED_ACTIVATION_TOKEN
    value: "<activation-token>"

worker:
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: true
      size: 1Gi
```

Install the worker Helm chart:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

### Token from a Kubernetes Secret

Store the activation token in a Kubernetes Secret and reference it using `secretRefs`. The chart injects the Secret value as the `BOUNDARY_WORKER_CONTROLLER_GENERATED_ACTIVATION_TOKEN` environment variable, which Boundary reads at startup via the `env://` prefix.

Create the Secret before installing the chart:

```shell-session
$ kubectl create secret generic boundary-worker-secrets \
  --namespace boundary \
  --from-literal=worker-controller-generated-activation-token='<activation-token>'
```

The key name (`worker-controller-generated-activation-token`) must match the value set in `secretRefs.keys.controllerGeneratedActivationToken` in your Helm values file. This command is provided as an example — use any Secret management method that fits your workflow.

Set `controller_generated_activation_token` to the `env://` reference in `worker.config`:

```hcl
worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]
  auth_storage_path = "/var/lib/boundary"
  controller_generated_activation_token = "env://BOUNDARY_WORKER_CONTROLLER_GENERATED_ACTIVATION_TOKEN"

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "controller-led"]
  }
}
```

Example values:

```yaml
secretRefs:
  secretName: boundary-worker-secrets
  keys:
    controllerGeneratedActivationToken: worker-controller-generated-activation-token

worker:
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: true
      size: 1Gi
```

Set `secretRefs.validateExisting=true` to make Helm fail early if the Secret is missing during installation.

<Note>

When `secretRefs.secretName` is set, the chart validates that `worker.config` uses the correct `env://` variable name for the secret-backed field. Using a different variable name causes the chart to fail during rendering before installation completes. The required name is:

- `env://BOUNDARY_WORKER_CONTROLLER_GENERATED_ACTIVATION_TOKEN` for `controller_generated_activation_token`

If you use a different variable name, the chart fails during rendering with an error message that identifies the field and the expected variable name. Hardcoding the token directly in `worker.config` when `secretRefs.secretName` is set is also rejected.

</Note>

Install the worker Helm chart:

```shell-session
$ helm install boundary-worker hashicorp/boundary-worker \
  --namespace boundary \
  --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml \
  --wait
```

## KMS (key management system)-backed worker authentication

Boundary only supports KMS-backed worker authentication in self-managed deployments. For more information, refer to [External KMS registration](/boundary/docs/workers/registration/kms). It is not available for HCP Boundary workers.

For self-managed deployments, configure the worker HCL with the required KMS worker-auth stanza. KMS authentication does not require persistent local auth material, so you should disable the auth storage PVC.

Example HCL for KMS-backed worker authentication:

```hcl
disable_mlock = true

listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9202"
  purpose = "proxy"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:9203"
  purpose       = "ops"
  tls_disable   = "{{ .Values.tls.ops.disabled }}"
  tls_cert_file = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.crt"
  tls_key_file  = "{{ .Values.tls.mountPath }}/tls.key"
}

worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "kms"]
  }
}

kms "aead" {
  purpose = "worker-auth"
  aead_type = "aes-gcm"
  key = "<base64-encoded-32-byte-key>"
  key_id = "<worker-auth-key-id>"
}

events {
  audit_enabled        = true
  sysevents_enabled    = true
  observations_enabled = true
  sink "stderr" {
    name        = "all-events"
    event_types = ["*"]
    format      = "cloudevents-json"
  }
}
```

```yaml
worker:
  persistence:
    authStorage:
      enabled: false
```

When `worker.persistence.authStorage.enabled` is `false`, the chart mounts an `emptyDir` at the auth storage path instead of creating a PVC. Its contents do not persist when the pod is replaced.

## Enable session recording storage

If the worker will store session recordings, enable recording persistence and set `recording_storage_path` in `worker.config`.

<Note>

RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) session recording exports require FFmpeg `5.1.0` or later and the `libsvtav1` codec. If your selected worker image does not include them, build a custom image that adds them and reference it in your values file.

Pass the custom image in your values file:

```yaml
image:
  repository: <your-registry>/boundary-worker
  tag: "1.0.0-ffmpeg"
```

</Note>

Example values:

```yaml
worker:
  persistence:
    recording:
      enabled: true
      size: 10Gi
      path: /boundary/recording
```

Matching HCL:

```hcl
worker {
  name = "boundary-worker"
  public_addr = ""
  initial_upstreams = ["boundary-controller-cluster:9201"]
  recording_storage_path = "/boundary/recording"

  tags {
    type = ["worker", "recording"]
  }
}
```

Ensure the recording storage path in `worker.config` matches `worker.persistence.recording.path`.

## Change service ports

You can change the proxy listener port. Update both the HCL and chart values when you do so.

Example values:

```yaml
worker:
  service:
    proxy:
      port: 9222
      targetPort: 9222
```

Matching HCL:

```hcl
listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:9222"
  purpose = "proxy"
}
```

The chart does not synchronize these settings automatically. Keep the operations listener and `worker.service.ops.targetPort` on `9203`: the Deployment hardcodes the named ops container port to `9203`, and the liveness and readiness probes target that named port. The Service-facing `worker.service.ops.port` may differ.

## Troubleshooting

### Session recordings fail to export

If session recording exports fail, confirm that the selected worker image includes FFmpeg `5.1.0` or later and the `libsvtav1` codec, as described in [Enable session recording storage](#enable-session-recording-storage).

## More information

To view supported Helm values so that you can configure or update workers, refer to [Worker values](/boundary/docs/deploy/helm-chart/worker-values).
